paragraphs: I do not intend to discuss every writer who has taken up the subject of female manners — that would in fact merely mean treading old ground, since in general they have all written in the same strain. But in attacking man’s much-boasted prerogative — which may emphatically be called the iron sceptre of tyranny, the original sin of tyrants — I declare my opposition to all power that rests on prejudices, however ancient.

If the submission demanded rests on justice, no appeal to any higher power is possible — for God is justice itself. So let us, as children of the same parent (unless being the younger born makes us bastards), reason together, and learn to yield to reason’s authority whenever her voice can be distinctly heard. But suppose it is shown that this throne of prerogative stands merely on a chaotic heap of prejudices with no inherent principle of order binding them together, or on an elephant, a tortoise, or even the mighty shoulders of a son of the earth. Then whoever dares to face the consequences may break free without failing in any duty, and without sinning against the order of things.

While reason raises man above the brutish herd, and death is pregnant with promises, only those who have no confidence in their own strength are subject to blind authority. “They are free who will be free!”*
(*Footnote. “He is the free man, whom TRUTH makes free!” Cowper.)

The being who can govern itself has nothing to fear in life; but if anything is dearer to it than its own self-respect, the price must be paid to the last penny. Virtue, like everything of value, must be loved for her own sake alone, or she will not come to dwell with us. She will not grant that peace “which passeth understanding” when she is merely used as stilts for reputation and observed with pharisaical exactness, because “honesty is the best policy.”

It cannot be denied that the plan of life which enables us to carry some knowledge and virtue into another world is the one best designed to secure contentment in this one; yet few people act on this principle, though everyone agrees that it is beyond dispute. Present pleasure, or present power, sweeps these sober convictions aside; and it is for the day, not for life, that man strikes his bargain with happiness. How few! how very few! have enough foresight or resolve to endure a small evil in the moment in order to avoid a greater one later.

Woman especially, whose virtue* rests on mutual prejudices, rarely reaches such greatness of mind; and so, enslaved to her own feelings, she is easily subdued by other people’s. Degraded like this, her reason — her misty reason! — serves to polish her chains rather than snap them.
(*Footnote. I mean to use a word that covers more than chastity, the sexual virtue.)
I have listened with indignation to women arguing along the same lines as men, and adopting the sentiments that brutalize them with all the stubbornness of ignorance.
Let me support what I say with a few examples. Mrs. Piozzi, who frequently repeated by rote things she did not understand, steps up with sentences rolled out in the style of Dr. Johnson.

“Seek not for happiness in singularity; and dread a refinement of wisdom as a deviation into folly.” So she dogmatically lectures a newly married man; and to explain this pompous opening, she adds, “I said that the person of your lady would not grow more pleasing to you, but pray let her never suspect that it grows less so: that a woman will pardon an affront to her understanding much sooner than one to her person, is well known; nor will any of us contradict the assertion. All our attainments, all our arts, are employed to gain and keep the heart of man; and what mortification can exceed the disappointment, if the end be not obtained: There is no reproof however pointed, no punishment however severe, that a woman of spirit will not prefer to neglect; and if she can endure it without complaint, it only proves that she means to make herself amends by the attention of others for the slights of her husband!”

Here are genuinely masculine sentiments. “All our ARTS are employed to gain and keep the heart of man:” — and what follows? — if her person should be neglected (and has any person, even one shaped with the proportions of the Medici Venus, ever escaped being slighted?), she will console herself by trying to please other men. Noble morality! Yet this is how the understanding of the entire sex is insulted, and how their virtue is stripped of the common foundation of all virtue. A woman ought to know that her husband cannot find her person as pleasing as her lover once did; and if she takes offence at him for being a human creature, she might as well whine over losing his heart as over any other foolish thing. Indeed, this very lack of discernment, or this unreasonable anger, shows that he was unable to turn his doting on her person into affection for her virtues or respect for her understanding.

As long as women profess such opinions and live by them, their understandings, at least, deserve the contempt and abuse which men — men WHO NEVER insult their persons — have pointedly directed at the female mind. And vain women thoughtlessly take up the sentiments of exactly these polite men, who have no wish to be encumbered with mind. They ought to realize, however, that only the reason they insult can throw around the person that SACRED reserve which makes human affections (and human affections always carry some base alloy) as lasting as is consistent with the grand purpose of existence — namely, the attainment of virtue.
